name: Prior Art and Clearance Searching
title: Prior Art and Clearance Searching
answer: Prior art and clearance searching is the work of finding what already exists before a patent is filed or a mark is adopted, so that a client knows what they are walking into. In patents, prior art searching looks for publications, patents and public uses that predate a claimed invention. In trademarks, clearance searching looks for earlier marks and uses that could block registration or invite an opposition. The two share a method, a paper trail and a purpose, which is to reduce surprise rather than to guarantee an outcome.

sections.body: Prior art and clearance searching is the work of finding what already exists before a patent is filed or a mark is adopted, so that a client knows what they are walking into. sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The work runs on large document collections: patent office registers, trademark registers, journal and conference literature, and the open web. Commercial databases such as Derwent, Orbit and PatBase sit alongside free sources like Google Patents, Espacenet and the USPTO and EUIPO registers. Classification systems, chiefly the Cooperative Patent Classification and the Nice classes for goods and services, are the main way a searcher turns a description of an invention or a brand into a workable query. Increasingly, semantic search and AI tools sit on top of these collections, but the underlying registers remain the record that matters.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: A search starts with an interview, because the client's own description of the invention or the mark is usually too narrow or too broad. The searcher builds a concept map, picks classifications and keywords, then runs iterative queries and reviews hits by hand. Results are ranked by relevance and closeness, and the output is a written opinion that sets out the closest references, what they disclose, and where the gaps are. For trademarks the exercise adds goods and services comparison and an assessment of likelihood of confusion. A search report is a snapshot of a moving register, so date, databases and queries are recorded.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Search results are privileged work product when done at the direction of counsel, and that protection depends on how the search is commissioned and who runs it. In patent matters, what a searcher finds and does not disclose can bear on inequitable conduct and on the duty of candour owed to the patent office. In trademark matters, a clearance opinion that is ignored can support a finding of wilful infringement, so the file needs to show what was known and when. Provenance matters throughout: which database, which version of a document, which date of access. This site tracks 92 intellectual property matters among 152 active AI lawsuits, a reminder that search and clearance work now sits close to live litigation.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: AI is changing the search itself, with semantic retrieval, embedding based similarity and automated classification suggestion reducing the mechanical part of the job. The harder shift is volume: as AI generated filings and AI assisted inventions multiply, the prior art corpus grows and the noise within it grows faster. Searchers are likely to spend less time finding documents and more time judging whether a document is a real disclosure, who authored it and when it became public. Expect clearance practice to lean further on continuous monitoring rather than one off searches, and expect the audit trail around AI assisted search to become part of the opinion itself.
